questions.qtext: A minimal super key (i.e, one of the super keys for which no proper subset is a superkey) is called:
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 2)

Answer is option $\boxed{\text{B. Candidate Key}}$

The question ask for which is minimal superkey.

A. Super key: Yes this could be the answer but Super Key need not always be minimal.

B. Candidate Key: This is the most suitable answer herre, Minimal Super key is called candidate Key

C. Primary key: This is not the answer because not every minimal key can be primary key , there can be only one primary key in the relation.

D. Both $C_k$ and $P_k$: This is not the answer here because for the same reason option C is not the answer.

Detailed Video Solution: https://youtu.be/eVgBJ1KImRY?t=615&feature=shared

Source of the question: https://gateoverflow.in/351374/nielit-scientific-assistant-a-2020-november-86

questions.qtext: If $R$ is a relation in Relational Data Model and $A_1,A_2,\dots A_n$ are the attributes of relation $R$, what is the cardinality of $R$ expressed in terms of domain of attributes?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Selected solution (score: 15)

A relation is a set of ordered tuples where the order of the attributes matter and the order of the tuples does not matter.

In set theory, the cross product between two sets produces ordered pairs. For example, take two sets $A, B$

$A \times B = \{ (a, b) \,\vert\, a \in A, b \in B \}$

The cross product of the two sets produces ordered pairs of the values from each set and every tuple is unique.

Here in a relation, the schema consists of the attributes and each of the values of the attributes are domain-restricted and atomic.

Each of the attribute in the relation has a domain from which the values are entered into the cell of the table.

Any valid instance of the relation $R$ is always a subset of the cross product of the domain values of the attributes.

$R \subseteq D_1 \times D_2 \times \cdots \times D_n$

There is a property in cross product of the sets $\mid A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n \mid = \mid A_1 \mid \times \mid A_2 \mid \times \cdots \mid A_n\mid$

The agenda of the question is to get the cardianlity of an instance of the relation, which can be expressed as $\mid R \mid$ .

Hence $\mid R \mid \subseteq \mid D_1 \times D_2 \times \cdots \times D_n \mid$

Option A is the answer.

Detailed Video Solution: https://youtu.be/eVgBJ1KImRY?t=1512&feature=shared

Source of the question: https://gateoverflow.in/336416/nielit-2017-july-scientist-b-it-section-b-19

Option A here we've to know cardinality of relational model R and degree of relational model,

$Cardinality \;of \;relational \; model$ : Number of tuples possible in the relation R

$Degree \;of \;relational \; model$ :Number of attributes in the relational model R which is actually defined when the schema was created.

So all the possible combinations can be calculated as product of cardinality of attribtutes. And the cardinality of R will always be less than or equal to the product
